one_liner: SIMD Rust-to-WASM port of es-module-lexer's lexer.c; same API and results, 4-18x faster parses in Node.
what_it_does: Finds the import and export statements of a JavaScript module (positions, specifiers, dynamic imports, import.meta), exactly like es-module-lexer 1.7.0, which bundlers and dev servers (Vite, Node loaders) call on every module. It is a drop-in: same exports (ImportType, init, initSync, parse), same result shapes and the same errors, installed under the original name with an npm alias ("es-module-lexer": "npm:@r1ck404/fast-es-module-lexer@1.7.2"). The original's asm.js subpath (es-module-lexer/js) is not provided.
how_it_is_fast: lexer.c is ported function by function to no_std Rust, but the main loop stops only at the characters that can change state (( ) { } ' " / ` and the pairs ex, im, cl); a SIMD nibble-table classifier (two u8x16_swizzle lookups per 16 bytes, the simdjson-style character classification) finds them 64 characters at a time, and lastTokenPos is derived from a non-whitespace mask instead of being updated per character. Strings, templates and comments are skipped with SIMD scans, the source is narrowed to one byte per UTF-16 unit, and it is copied into WASM memory at memcpy speed (Buffer.latin1Write/ucs2Write in Node, a js-string-builtins WASM loop in Chromium, TextEncoder.encodeInto elsewhere) instead of the original's charCodeAt loop into a Uint16Array. Results return as one Int32Array rather than one WASM call per field, and specifiers without escapes are sliced instead of eval'd.
when_to_use: Dev servers, bundlers and module loaders that lex many ES modules per build or page load (batches of real package files ran 5-8x faster in Node, 3.5-4.4x in Chromium).
Large single bundles of 0.5-1.2 MB, where the SIMD skip-ahead pays most (6-18x in Node, 4.9-7.1x in Chromium on the published run; the low end is a non-ASCII file that takes the UTF-16 path).
In-browser Node runtimes or web IDEs on V8, where the js-string-builtins copy path avoids the slow TextEncoder in Blink.
Any project already on es-module-lexer 1.7.x that can add an npm alias: no code change and identical results, including the original's quirks.
when_not_to_use: Engines without WebAssembly SIMD (older Safari, some embedded runtimes): there is no scalar or asm.js fallback.
Size-critical browser bundles: { initSync, parse } bundles to 21.6 KB minified / 9.3 KB gzip vs 14.1 / 6.5 KB for es-module-lexer, mostly the 16.6 KB WASM.

Projects on es-module-lexer 2.x or 3.x (3.0.3 is current): only 1.7.0 is mirrored, and upstream has since added its own speedups (2.3.1 fast native UTF-16 copy into WASM memory on Node, 2.3.2 bulk skipping of identifier and number runs, 3.0.0 SIMD scanning of long comments and templates, one-import parse 354 to 238 ns), so the gap to current upstream is smaller than the published ratios and unmeasured.
Teams that need a maintained, widely used dependency: one author, 1 star, no issues filed, under three weeks old, and the npm latest (1.7.3) is not in the GitHub repository.
Workloads that re-parse an identical string expecting cold-parse cost (benchmarks, profiling): since 1.7.2 the package returns a cached scan for repeated sources of 4,096-1,048,576 code units.

integration.form: module (npm package @r1ck404/fast-es-module-lexer; one ESM file with the WASM embedded as base64, plus browser.mjs selected by the browser export condition)
integration.dependencies: none at run time (Rust wasm32 toolchain and binaryen only to rebuild the WASM)
integration.min_toolchain: Node 18+ (engines field); any engine with WebAssembly SIMD (simd128); rebuild needs rustc with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target (version not pinned) and binaryen ^132
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host with SIMD: Node, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit (browser test suite runs in all three); Deno and Bun take the TextEncoder or builtins copy path
integration.thread_safety: not documented; one module-level WASM instance and a module-level cache per JS realm, so each worker gets its own (JS is single-threaded per realm)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same exports, results and errors as es-module-lexer 1.7.0 and installed under its name, but no /js asm.js subpath, it needs WASM SIMD, and malformed inputs on which the original reads outside its source are answered as a fresh original instance would (deterministic), and nesting deeper than 1024 brackets / 512 import( calls is handled where the original goes wrong

gotchas: Benchmark caveat: commit 7df1749 (2026-09-30, release 1.7.2) added a one-entry cache that reuses the last WASM scan when the identical string (4,096-1,048,576 UTF-16 units) is parsed again; the repo's bench/es-module-lexer.bench.mjs parses the same f.code string in a loop, so rerunning it on the current code times cache hits (result-object construction only) for the 51 KB, 513-536 KB, 948 KB and 1 MB single-file rows. The published numbers (results file of 2026-09-28) predate the cache; the batch rows (different files in turn) and the 70 B, 1.6 KB and 9 MB rows fall outside it, and three.module (1.2 MB) only if it exceeds 1,048,576 code units.

The npm latest 1.7.3 (published 2026-09-30 19:09 UTC) has no matching commit: the repo stops at 1.7.2, yet 1.7.3 ships a different init (compile-only, instance created on first parse), a JS text decoder instead of the 356-byte decoder module, and the older 1.7.1 WASM binary rather than 1.7.2's.

The Rust toolchain is not pinned: lib.rs and build.mjs are byte-identical between c59fa38 and HEAD, yet 1.7.1 and 1.7.2 embed different WASM binaries (22,068 vs 22,408 base64 characters), so a rebuild will not reproduce the measured module bit for bit.

Deliberate behaviour differences on malformed code (documented): very deep nesting and record overflows are answered as a fresh original instance would, so results can differ from a long-lived es-module-lexer instance whose answer depends on earlier parses.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over es-module-lexer (the catalogued baseline) when parse time of many or large modules matters and the host has WASM SIMD; keep es-module-lexer when bundle size, the asm.js fallback or a long track record matter more. No other ES-module lexer is catalogued; the general WASM siblings (sax-wasm, markdown-wasm, source-map) solve different problems.
verified_claims_summary: First-party run on a Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Node 24.16 and headless Chromium 149, alternating fresh processes and keeping the best of 3 per-process medians: es-module-lexer 1.7.0's C-to-WASM build vs this SIMD Rust WASM port took 2.11 ms vs 0.117 ms on react-dom-client.production (536 KB, 18.1x; 7.1x in Chromium), 4.6 vs 0.7 us on a 1.6 KB module (6.6x), 34.6 vs 4.7 ms on typescript.js (9 MB, 7.4x) and 2.51 vs 0.32 ms on 644 lodash-es modules (7.9x; 4.2x in Chromium). Speedups include the faster source copy into WASM memory, not only the lexer. The baseline is es-module-lexer 1.7.0 (April 2025), two majors and several upstream performance releases behind the 3.0.x current when the package was made.
status_note: Active but brand new (37 commits, 2026-09-26 to 2026-10-01, single author, 1 star, no issues), MIT-licensed and installable by npm alias; it mirrors a stale es-module-lexer 1.7.0, the shipped npm 1.7.3 is not reproducible from the repository, and the current code caches repeated parses, so re-benchmark on your own varied inputs against current es-module-lexer before relying on the published ratios.
